narrative:
Your application for promotion was denied because the model estimates a 57% chance you will leave the company in the near future. This is not a judgment on your performance or potential; in fact, factors such as your gender, age, and health were deliberately left out. Instead, the prediction looks at patterns from employees like you to assess retention risk. Among the many factors considered, three stand out as most important.

Your training history is the strongest factor and it works in your favor. You attended seven or more training programs in the last three years, which is more than many employees who stay—only about one in five of them have that level of participation. This suggests you are engaged and growing, so this part of your profile pulls toward staying.

However, your overall experience and your tenure here push in the opposite direction. You have six to ten years of total experience, a range that is less common among employees who remain than the one-to-five-year group. More importantly, you have only been in your current organization for one to five years. That relatively short time in this job, combined with substantial experience overall, often signals that a person is likely to move on—perhaps because they feel they can find another role easily.

The result is a balance slightly tipped toward leaving: your strong training record is not enough to offset the risk from your experience and tenure. If you believe this risk is wrong, you can speak with HR about your career intentions. The organization, in turn, should consider whether this promotion decision would itself make an experienced, well-trained employee more likely to leave.
